newsitem.title: USA: Whitewater figure McDougal enters federal prison.
newsitem.headline: Whitewater figure McDougal enters federal prison.

text.p: James McDougal, President Bill Clinton's one-time partner in the Whitewater real estate deal, entered a federal prison medical centre on Monday to begin serving a three-year sentence for fraud and conspiracy.
A spokesman for the Bureau of Prisons said McDougal arrived at the Federal Medical Centre in Lexington at about 10 a.m. (1400 GMT). The facility has 1,467 prisoners.
McDougal has had a stroke, has a blocked carotid artery and has a heart condition that requires daily doses of nitroglycerin.
Claudia Riley, his friend and landlady, said on Sunday that his "attitude is very good. He's telling everyone that this is just another of life's adventures and that he'll get through it."
He has also been quoted as saying he may work on his memoirs while in prison. He may be eligible for parole in two and one-half years.

McDougal went to jail leaving questions about the information he has provided investigators regarding Clinton and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton. McDougal's wife Susan has been in jail since September for refusing to answer questions from a special grand jury investigating the affair.

The McDougals and the Clintons were investors in the 1970s in the Whitewater real estate venture in Arkansas, which was underwritten by a financial institution McDougal owned. The project and McDougal's firm, Madison Guaranty Savings and Loan, both failed, costing taxpayers an estimated $60 million.

Special Whitewater prosecutor Kenneth Starr is trying to determine whether deposits from Madison Guaranty were diverted to the Whitewater real estate development. The McDougals and former Arkansas Gov. Jim Guy Tucker were convicted in May 1996 after a three-month trial in Little Rock in which Clinton testified for the defence on videotape.

McDougal, convicted of 19 counts of fraud and conspiracy, could have received more than 80 years in prison, but within months of the verdict he began cooperating with prosecutors, resulting in a greatly reduced sentence.
After his sentencing, he backed away from his earlier insistence that the Clintons were guilty of no wrongdoing. "I wouldn't go to the bank on that," McDougal said.

In recent interviews, he has hinted that Mrs. Clinton committed perjury before a Whitewater grand jury in Washington when she testified she had done minimal work for another McDougal real estate project.
